pedagogy.summary: For 5–7s this topic pairs each of the five senses with its body part and with what it DETECTS: sight/eyes detect light, hearing/ears detect sound, touch/skin detects pressure and temperature, taste/tongue detects flavours, smell/nose detects smells. It is best taught experientially — children USE each sense on real objects (a feely bag, listening games, tasting, smelling jars) and name the sense, the organ and what it picked up. The step beyond naming is the idea that each sense detects a different KIND of information about the world, and that senses often work together (taste and smell especially). Keep it hands-on and everyday; the objective is confident matching of sense–organ–stimulus plus real examples, not anatomy of the eye or ear (those come later). This also feeds the brain topic: senses are how the brain finds out about the world.
bestPractices: Lead with direct experience: feely bags, sound-guessing, smell jars, taste tests, spotting things — children use the sense, then name it, its organ and what it detected.
Make the sense–organ–stimulus triple explicit for each (eyes–light, ears–sound, skin–pressure/temperature, tongue–flavour, nose–smell), the core matching objective.
Show senses working TOGETHER — e.g. hold your nose while tasting and flavour fades — so children see the senses as a team informing the brain.
Anchor to safety and daily life (smelling smoke, feeling something too hot) so each sense has a purpose, not just a label.
Keep detail age-appropriate — no receptor or wave physics; 'ears detect sounds', 'eyes detect light' is enough at this stage.
keyRepresentations: Five sense–organ–stimulus cards (eye/light, ear/sound, skin/pressure & temperature, tongue/flavour, nose/smell)
Hands-on stations: feely bag, sound jars, smell pots, taste trays, spot-it pictures
A child-figure with the five sense organs highlighted
Everyday-use examples matched to each sense
commonMisconceptions: 'We have exactly five senses and that's all' — fine as an age-appropriate model, but balance and body-position senses exist too (keep as a light aside).
'Taste comes only from the tongue' — missing that smell contributes much of flavour.
'Skin only feels touch' — missing that it also detects temperature and pain.
'You hear/see with your brain-eyes' — confusing the organ that detects with the brain that interprets; the organ detects, the brain makes sense of it.
'The tongue has zones for each taste' — the old 'tongue map' myth; tastes are detected all over the tongue.
'Senses work separately' — not seeing that they combine to build one picture of the world.

learn.summary: For children aged 5–7, teach the five senses as a sense–organ–stimulus triple: eyes detect light, ears detect sound, skin detects pressure and temperature, tongue detects flavours, nose detects smells. Lead with direct experience at hands-on stations, then have children name the sense, the body part, and what it picked up. Beyond naming, build the idea that each sense detects a different KIND of information and that senses often work together (especially taste and smell for flavour). Keep it everyday and age-appropriate — no eye/ear anatomy or wave physics yet. This also lays groundwork for the idea that all senses report to the brain.

activities.title: Sense stations: use it, then name it
feedback: If a child names the organ but not what it detects, prompt: 'Your eyes — but what do eyes pick up?' (light) and 'Your ears pick up…?' (sound).
If a child leaves out touch/skin, hand them the feely-bag object: 'What is your skin telling you — can you name two things, like bumpy, cold, or wet?'
Confirm correct triples by repeating them back: 'Yes — nose, smell, you smelled the flowers.'
activities.rationale: Direct experience before labelling suits this age and anchors the sense–organ–stimulus matching objective, which is the core target. The curriculum asks pupils to say which body part is associated with each sense.
sourceClaims: KS1 pupils should identify, name, draw and label the basic parts of the human body and say which part of the body is associated with each sense.
learnerActions: Visit hands-on stations and USE each sense before naming it: a feely bag (reach in and feel without looking), sound jars or a listening game, smell pots, a taste tray, and spot-it pictures.
After each station, say three things aloud: the sense used, the body part (organ) that detected it, and WHAT it picked up — e.g. 'touch, my skin, it felt bumpy and cold'.
Match five cards that pair each sense to its organ and to an everyday example: eyes catch a rainbow, ears catch a barking dog, skin feels warm sand, tongue tastes lemon, nose smells baking.
activities.intendedInsight: Each sense uses a particular body part to detect a different kind of information about the world.

activities.title: Senses team up: the nose-hold taste test
feedback: If a child predicts the tongue alone will manage and is surprised, name it: 'The flavour faded because smell helps taste — they team up.'

If a child says taste and smell are the same sense, separate them: the nose detects smells (odours in the air), the tongue detects tastes like sweet, sour, salty and bitter; together they make the full flavour of food, but they are different senses.
Link to daily life: 'That's why an orange tastes boring when you have a very blocked-up nose with a cold.'
activities.rationale: A predict-then-test contrast with a surprising result targets the misconception that taste comes only from the tongue and shows taste and smell working as a team. An optional 'hold your nose' toggle that dims the on-screen taste is one way to represent the same idea when real food is not available; it supplements the real tasting rather than standing in for it.
learnerActions: Before tasting, predict: 'If I pinch my nose shut, will I still tell these two flavours apart?' Say why you think so.
Taste two foods with the same texture but different flavours (e.g. two jellybean flavours, or finely grated apple and pear) with the nose pinched, then again with the nose open, and compare.
Say what changed and which two senses were working together.
activities.intendedInsight: Taste and smell cooperate: much of flavour comes from smell, so for flavour the tongue does not do the job by itself — these two senses combine to build the taste you recognise. (This is about flavour specifically; other senses can still work on their own.)

activities.title: Tongue-map myth buster
feedback: If a child expects a specific zone, invite them to test the same flavour on another part: 'Can you still taste it here?'
Affirm the corrected idea and tie it back: 'Taste buds all around your tongue can pick up every kind of taste — there are no special zones. Taste is one of our five senses.'
activities.rationale: Actively testing the myth replaces a wrong belief with a checked observation rather than just asserting the correction. A lift-the-flap representation is an optional way to reveal this when direct tasting is impractical.
sourceClaims: The classic 'tongue map' (separate zones for each taste) is a myth; different tastes are detectable across the whole tongue.
learnerActions: Taste a strong flavour (e.g. something sour or salty) touched to different parts of the tongue, such as the tip and each side.
Notice whether you can taste the same flavour in each place you tried, not just in one 'zone'.
State the myth and the correction in your own words: 'There are no separate zones for each taste.'
activities.intendedInsight: The old 'tongue map' (separate zones for each taste) is a myth: taste buds on the tip, sides and back of the tongue can each pick up all the basic tastes. The middle has fewer taste buds, so tastes can feel weaker there.

activities.title: Which sense would help? Reasoning game
feedback: Full answer to the orange task: smell (nose picks up the odour), taste (tongue detects sweet and sour tastes), and touch (skin/fingers feel the bumpy peel and the wet, juicy inside) can identify it; hearing wouldn't help much; sight fails because eyes need light and are covered.
If a child lists only eyes, ears, nose, tongue and omits skin, add touch as a full sense: the skin detects pressure, texture, and temperature — feel the peel to show it.
If a child names organs but not what each detects, pair each: eyes–light, ears–sound, nose–smell, tongue–taste, skin–touch/temperature.

Optional deeper probe: 'If the room were pitch dark and you were blindfolded, would smell still work — and why doesn't smell need light the way sight does?' (Smell picks up odours in the air, so it doesn't rely on light.)
activities.rationale: Applying the triples to a novel situation checks understanding beyond recall and surfaces gaps (omitting touch, merging taste and smell). Dragging a stimulus to its sense turns naming into active play; the 'how do you know it's raining' prompt folds in the optional guessing-game conversation as a reasoning hook.
learnerActions: Blindfolded, hold a slice of orange and work out which senses could still tell you it's an orange, and what each one would be picking up.
Explain why your EYES can't help right now (they need light and are covered).
Try a drag-and-match: move stimuli (a bell, a flower, an ice cube) to the sense that detects each, and answer 'how do you know it's raining without looking?'
activities.intendedInsight: Different senses detect different information, so you can pick the right sense for a situation and explain when one (like sight) can't help.

constraints: Keep detail age-appropriate: 'eyes detect light', 'ears detect sounds' is enough — no receptor biology or wave physics at this stage; eye/ear anatomy comes later.
Treat 'we have exactly five senses' as an age-appropriate model; balance and body-position senses exist too and can be mentioned as a light aside, not corrected as an error.
Distinguish the organ that detects from the brain that interprets: the organ detects, the brain makes sense of it.
Anchor each sense to a purpose in safety and daily life (smelling smoke, feeling something too hot) so senses are not just labels.

Tap-to-reveal figures, drag-to-match games, flaps and nose-hold toggles are scaffolds carrying pre-authored facts: they can present and check the matching but do not themselves make a child actually smell, taste or feel a real object. Because the objective includes experiencing what each sense detects, pair these scaffolds with hands-on use of real senses on real objects; which medium is more effective has not been tested here. A matching or quiz check assesses recognition, which alone does not show a child can produce or apply the ideas, so it should follow hands-on exploration.
Hold safety and allergy awareness in any taste/smell activity (food sensitivities, hygiene, supervised tasting).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; the two cited sources were not re-fetched and were already marked verified:false in the source. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source's catalogue judgements that '3D adds no value' and that naming is 'best done visually/experientially' are fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws; they have been dropped rather than asserted. The tap-to-reveal figure is retained as one representation, not the uniquely correct medium.

The source assessment text once writes 'ears detect sound waves'; for 5–7s the simpler 'ears detect sound' is used in activities to match the stated age-appropriate guidance, while the fuller phrasing is noted here as the source's own wording.

A non-preferred 'conversation' alternative (a character asking how you know it's raining without looking) was folded into the reasoning activity as an optional prompt rather than kept as a separate approach.
Activity 2's intended insight is scoped to flavour (taste+smell) so it does not imply, against activity 4, that a single sense can never identify something alone.
Independent re-audit: no critical learner-facing errors found; remaining uncertainty is about source/efficacy evidence only, held in the uncertain and review notes.

assess.poeTask: Give the child two similar strong-flavoured foods (e.g. a piece of apple and a piece of pear, or two jellybean flavours). Ask them to predict whether they'll still tell the flavours apart while pinching their nose shut, and WHY, before trying. Most predict the tongue alone will manage; with the nose pinched the flavours are surprisingly hard to distinguish — revealing whether they realise smell and taste work together.
probeDeeper: Why does an orange taste boring and hard to recognise when you have a very blocked-up nose with a cold?
If the room were pitch dark AND you were blindfolded, would smell still work? Why doesn't smell need light the way sight does?
What is your skin detecting when you feel the orange — can you name two things, like bumpy, cold, or wet?
assess.correctAnswer: With eyes blindfolded, sight can't help because it needs light and your eyes are covered. But smell (nose picking up the orange's odour), taste (tongue detecting its flavour), and touch (skin and fingers feeling the bumpy peel and wetness) can still identify it — each sense detects a different kind of information. Hearing wouldn't help much here. Each sense uses a different body part to detect a different thing.

errorPatterns.pattern: Taste and smell are the same sense, or one organ does both.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate them: the nose detects smells (odours in the air), the tongue detects tastes (flavours in food); they cooperate but are different senses.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Merges the nose and tongue, or names one sense for both jobs.

errorPatterns.pattern: Touch (skin) isn't really one of the senses.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Add touch as a full sense: the skin detects pressure, texture, and temperature — feel the peel to show it.
errorPatterns.distractor: Only smell and taste could tell — touch isn't one of the senses.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Lists only eyes, ears, nose, tongue; omits skin/touch.

errorPatterns.pattern: Names the sense organs but can't say what each one detects (eyes→light, ears→sound, etc.).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pair each organ with its stimulus: eyes–light, ears–sound, nose–smell, tongue–taste, skin–touch/temperature.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Matches organ to sense but not the sense to the specific thing it picks up.

responseLevels.gap: Can't match senses to organs or to what they detect; merges taste and smell, or leaves out touch.
responseLevels.full: Matches each sense to its organ and to the specific thing it detects (light, sound, flavour, odour, pressure/temperature) and reasons about which senses can or can't help in a given situation.
responseLevels.partial: Names the five senses and organs but is shaky on what each detects, or gives everyday examples without linking organ to stimulus consistently.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You're blindfolded and someone hands you a slice of orange. Which of your senses could still tell you it's an orange, and what would each one be picking up? And why can't your EYES help you right now?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who leaves out touch, or merges taste and smell, or can't say what each sense detects, reveals the gap. Only a child who maps sense→organ→what-it-detects can pick the right senses for a blindfolded task and explain why sight fails. The tier-two 'what would each be picking up' forces the organ-to-stimulus link.
